findings.title: CRASH: every two-char relational operator (<=, >=, ==, !=) crashes the compiler (SIGILL)
findings.description: parse_relation() feeds the second character of a two-char relational operator into type_checker->feed_in_tokens(), which (once two tokens are buffered) calls Typechecker::second_relation_token_chains(). That function's switch statement (T_ASSIGN/T_COLON/T_EXCLAM/T_GREATER/T_LESS cases) only 'break's and never returns a value for the 'valid chain' case -- the trailing 'return true;' is commented out (line 242) -- so control falls off the end of a non-bool function, which is undefined behavior. Empirically this produces SIGILL. Reproduced with a minimal program using 'x >= 3', 'x <= 3', 'x == 3', and 'x != 3' inside an if-condition; gdb backtrace: Typechecker::second_relation_token_chains (Typechecker.cpp:227) <- Typechecker::feed_in_tokens (Typechecker.cpp:98) <- parser::parse_relation (parser.cpp:2264) <- parser::parse_arithOp <- parser::parse_expression <- parser::parse_if_statement. Confirmed by GCC itself: 'g++ -c Typechecker.cpp -Wreturn-type' emits 'Typechecker.cpp:243:1: warning: control reaches end of non-void function'. Because the trigger site (feeding the second operator character) is inside parser::parse_relation (parser.cpp:2264, and similarly 2198/2247), this crash is directly and trivially reachable from ordinary, spec-compliant relational expressions -- essentially any program comparing values with <=, >=, ==, or != crashes the whole compiler.

findings.title: CRASH: return statement with a 'compatible but not equal' type crashes the compiler (SIGILL)
findings.description: Typechecker::check_return_statement, called directly from parser::parse_return_statement (parser.cpp:1933), has a code path with no return statement: when the destination/procedure types are 'compatible' (per token_types_compatible_at_all) but not identical (e.g. returning an integer expression from a procedure declared to return bool -- explicitly declared 'compatible' by spec rule 14), the else-branch's inner 'if (token_one_type == token_two_type) return true;' has no corresponding else, so the function falls off the end -- undefined behavior, reproducibly SIGILL. Reproduced with 'procedure isPos : bool (variable p : integer) begin return p; end procedure;' (p is integer, procedure declared bool -- a legal, spec-compatible combination). gdb backtrace: Typechecker::check_return_statement (Typechecker.cpp:1211) <- parser::parse_return_statement (parser.cpp:1933) <- parser::parse_base_statement (parser.cpp:1511) <- parser::parse_procedure_body. Confirmed by GCC: 'Typechecker.cpp:1211:1: warning: control reaches end of non-void function'.

findings.title: parse_argument_list never consumes the comma, breaking all multi-argument procedure calls
findings.description: The grammar '<argument_list> ::= <expression> , <argument_list> | <expression>' requires consuming the literal comma. parse_argument_list detects T_COMMA and immediately recurses into parse_argument_list() WITHOUT calling Get_Valid_Token() first, so the recursive call re-enters with Current_parse_token still equal to the comma. That flows down through parse_expression -> parse_arithOp -> parse_relation -> parse_term -> parse_factor, none of which accept a comma as a factor start, producing 'Invalid token for factor discovered'. Confirmed: 'a := foo(1, 2, 3);' (with foo taking any number of args) fails to parse with exactly this cascade ('Invalid token for factor discovered', 'Error in expression', 'Missing ")" for the end of a procedure call'), while a single-argument call 'foo(1)' parses fine. Any procedure call with 2+ comma-separated arguments is unparseable.

findings.title: Procedure calls have zero undeclared-identifier, arity, or argument-type checking
findings.description: parse_procedure_call() only checks for '(' [args] ')' syntax; it never looks up the identifier in the symbol table (no I_PROCEDURE check), never compares the number of parsed arguments against the callee's declared parameter list, and never compares argument types against parameter types. parse_argument_list similarly discards each argument's resolved_token/type after parsing (no accumulation into a list for comparison). grep over Typechecker.cpp confirms there is no I_PROCEDURE / procedure_params / arity-related logic anywhere in the codebase. Empirically confirmed: with 'procedure foo : integer (variable p : integer) ... end procedure;', all three of `a := foo();` (0 args vs 1 required), `a := foo("hello");` (string arg vs integer param), and `a := bar(1);` (bar is completely undeclared) parse with 'no errors'. This directly violates spec semantic rule 8: 'The type signatures of a procedures arguments must match exactly their parameter declaration.'
findings.evidence: parser.cpp:2550-2618 (parse_argument_list / parse_procedure_call) contain no symbol-table lookups or type comparisons. Empirical: program with foo() (arity 0 vs required 1), foo("hello") (string vs required integer), and bar(1) (bar never declared) all parse with 'The program parsed successfully with no errors'.

findings.title: Unary minus on a numeric literal checks the wrong token-type constants and fails to parse
findings.description: In parse_factor's T_MINUS branch, after consuming '-', the code checks `Current_parse_token_type == T_INTEGER_TYPE || Current_parse_token_type == T_FLOAT_TYPE` -- these are the reserved-word type-keyword token types ('integer'/'float', values 268/269) -- instead of `T_INTEGER_VALUE || T_FLOAT_VALUE` (actual numeric-literal token types, values 279/280). A literal like -5 therefore always fails this check and falls into the final else, reporting 'Unexpected negative factor is not a name or a number'. This bug is masked at the very start of a top-level expression because parse_arithOp has its own leading '+'/'-' handling that consumes the minus before parse_factor ever sees it, so 'a := -5;' happens to parse (via a different, dead-code-ish code path in parse_arithOp, see related finding). However, whenever '-' appears after '*', '/', or a relational operator -- where parse_term/parse_relation call parse_factor() directly -- the real bug fires. Confirmed with '3 * -5' and 'x > -1', both producing 'Unexpected negative factor is not a name or a number' plus a cascade of secondary errors.

findings.title: Parenthesized sub-expressions never propagate their resolved_token/type out of parse_factor
findings.description: parse_factor's T_LPARAM branch parses the inner expression via parse_expression() and copies only `valid_parse`, never `factor_parse.resolved_token = expression_parse.resolved_token;`. The function falls through to the generic `factor_parse.valid_parse = valid_parse; return factor_parse;` at the end, so `factor_parse.resolved_token` is left as a default-constructed token (type=0, and `identifier_data_type` is not default-initialized in token.h, so it holds indeterminate/garbage data). Because parse_term/parse_relation/parse_arithOp/parse_expression each just forward 'the last operand's resolved_token' upward (see related finding on resolved_token propagation), a parenthesized relational expression used as an if/loop condition loses its type entirely. Confirmed: 'if ((x > 3)) then ... end if;' (plain double parens, no boolean operators involved) spuriously reports 'If statements must resolve to either type Bool or Integer', even though `x > 3` alone (unparenthesized) parses/typechecks with no error. The developer's own comment at the site ('what to do here? COME BACK ... maybe have parse_expression return a token of the type it resolves to?') acknowledges this was never finished.

findings.title: Procedure-call-as-factor also never sets its resolved_token, losing the call's return type
findings.description: In parse_factor's T_IDENTIFIER branch, when Next_parse_token_type == T_LPARAM (a procedure call used as a factor), the code calls parse_procedure_call() and assigns only `valid_parse`; `factor_parse.resolved_token` is never set, so -- like the parenthesized-expression case -- a default-constructed/garbage token bubbles up as the call's 'type'. Confirmed with a bool-returning procedure used directly as an if-condition ('if (isPos(5)) then ... end if;'): the if-statement type check spuriously fails with 'If statements must resolve to either type Bool or Integer', matching the exact failure signature of the parenthesized-expression bug, i.e. the procedure call's actual (bool) return type never reaches check_if_statement.

findings.title: parse_term does not loop/self-recurse for chained * or / (a * b * c fails to parse)
findings.description: The grammar '<term> ::= <term> * <factor> | <term> / <factor> | <factor>' is left-recursive and permits arbitrary chains. parse_term's continuation logic, after parsing the first factor, consumes a single '*'/'/' and calls parse_factor() directly (not parse_term() or a loop), so it can absorb at most ONE additional factor. A third consecutive '*'/'/' is left unconsumed. Contrast with parse_arithOp, which correctly self-recurses ('relation_parse = parse_arithOp();') to support arbitrarily long '+'/'-' chains. Confirmed empirically: '1 + 2 + 3 + 4' parses with no errors, but '1 * 2 * 3' fails with 'Missing ";" to end program statement', and '2 * 3 * 4 + 1' fails the same way. This breaks a very common construct (chained multiplication/division).

findings.title: parse_expression silently accepts a leading/duplicated '&' or '|' with a missing operand
findings.description: Grammar '<expression> ::= <expression> & <arithOp> | <expression> | <arithOp> | [not] <arithOp>' never allows '&'/'|' as a leading token (only 'not' or nothing may prefix an expression). parse_expression's own top-of-function if-chain nevertheless treats T_AMPERSAND/T_VERTICAL_BAR exactly like a valid entry, consuming the operator and parsing an arithOp for the remainder, with no error about a missing left operand. This branch is normally unreachable on well-formed input (callers/self-recursion always leave Current_parse_token at the start of a genuine arithOp/'not'), but on malformed input it silently 'succeeds': `a := & 5;` parses with no error. Worse, because the self-recursive continuation (line 2051-2052) consumes one '&'/'|' and then re-enters parse_expression() -- which again accepts a further leading '&'/'|' via the same branch -- a doubled operator with no operand between them is also silently accepted: `a := b & & 5;` parses with no error at all.

findings.title: parse_relation silently accepts a leading relational operator with a missing left operand
findings.description: Grammar '<relation> ::= relation < term | ... | term' never allows a relational operator to begin a relation. parse_relation's top-of-function if/else-if chain (T_LESS/T_GREATER/T_ASSIGN('==')/T_EXCLAM('!=')) nevertheless treats these as a legitimate entry point, consuming the operator and parsing a term for the right side, without reporting a missing-left-operand error. Confirmed: `a := < 5;` (with no left operand at all before '<') parses with 'no errors'.

findings.title: parse_relation's leading '!' branch can use an uninitialized bool and never consumes the trailing '=' or right term
findings.description: When parse_relation is entered with a leading T_EXCLAM (see related leading-operator finding), the code consumes '!' then checks `if (Current_parse_token_type != T_ASSIGN)` and reports an error only in that failure case; there is NO else branch to handle the valid '!=' case (parsing the trailing '=' and the right-hand term). In that (unhandled) case, `valid_parse` -- declared uninitialized at the top of the function -- is never assigned before it is read at `relation_parse.valid_parse = valid_parse;` a few lines later, and `term_parse`/Current_parse_token are also left untouched (the '=' remains unconsumed), corrupting the token stream for the caller. Confirmed by GCC -O2 -Wmaybe-uninitialized: "'valid_parse' may be used uninitialized" at parser.cpp:2278 (declared at parser.cpp:2152). Also confirmed to cause a cascade of misleading downstream errors ('If statements must resolve to either type Bool or Integer', 'Missing ")"', 'Missing ":" needed for assignment statement', 'Missing expected keyword "then"') for a program using 'if (!= x) then'.

findings.title: Leading '==' branch in parse_relation never consumes the second '=' before calling parse_term
findings.description: In the (reachable-on-malformed-input) leading T_ASSIGN branch, after consuming the first '=' and confirming the next token is also T_ASSIGN, the code feeds that second token to the typechecker but never calls Get_Valid_Token() to advance past it before invoking parse_term() -- unlike the equivalent, correctly-written logic later in the same function (lines 2241-2251) which does call Get_Valid_Token() for both '=' characters. This means parse_term() would be entered with Current_parse_token still pointing at the second '=', which cannot start a valid term/factor.

findings.title: A bare '!' (without '=') is silently accepted as a valid relational operator
findings.description: Spec only defines '!=' as a relational operator; a standalone '!' is not part of the <relation> grammar. In parse_relation's (normally reachable) post-term operator branch, T_LESS/T_GREATER/T_EXCLAM are all handled identically: if the following token is '=', it's consumed as part of a two-char operator; otherwise the code falls into an 'else' that simply calls parse_term() anyway -- which is correct for '<' and '>' (both valid standalone operators) but incorrect for '!' (never valid standalone). Confirmed: 'a := 5 ! 3;' (using a bare '!' where '!=' was presumably intended) parses with 'no errors', silently treating '!' as if it were '!='.

findings.title: resolved_token propagation only ever carries the last-parsed operand's token; operator results/left operands are silently dropped
findings.description: At every layer of the expression grammar chain, the returned token_and_status.resolved_token is simply copied from whichever sub-call was parsed LAST, never synthesized from the operator + both operands: parse_expression (line 2062) takes `arithop_parse.resolved_token` (the rightmost arithOp in a &/| chain); parse_arithOp (line 2139) takes `relation_parse.resolved_token` (the rightmost relation in a +/- chain); parse_relation (line 2279) takes `term_parse.resolved_token` (the right-hand term of a relational comparison, or the sole term if none); parse_term (line 2332) takes `factor_parse.resolved_token` (the right-hand factor of a */ operation). This means the 'type' bubbled up to statement-level checks (check_assignment_statement/check_if_statement/check_return_statement) is just the raw token of one operand (the left operand, and the operator's semantics, are discarded), not a computed result type for the operator (e.g., a relational comparison should conceptually resolve to bool, but its resolved_token is the right-hand term's own token/type). This is a structural root cause behind several concrete mischecks found separately (e.g., the parenthesized-expression and procedure-call-factor bugs where the 'last operand' is a garbage default token). Statement-level callers in parser.cpp (parse_if_statement/parse_loop_statement/parse_return_statement) work around part of this by re-looking the resolved_token's stringValue up in the symbol table, which only helps when the bubbled-up token happens to be a bare, unresolved identifier name.
findings.evidence: parser.cpp:2062 `expression_parse.resolved_token = arithop_parse.resolved_token;`; parser.cpp:2139 `arithop_parse.resolved_token = relation_parse.resolved_token;`; parser.cpp:2279 `relation_parse.resolved_token = term_parse.resolved_token;`; parser.cpp:2332 `term_parse.resolved_token = factor_parse.resolved_token;`. Workaround pattern e.g. parser.cpp:1645-1649 in parse_if_statement: `if (Lexer->symbol_table.scope_table[current_scope_id].is_in_table(expression_parse.resolved_token.stringValue)) { Context_token = update_context_token(Lexer->symbol_table.scope_table[current_scope_id].scope_map[expression_parse.resolved_token.stringValue]); updated_token = Context_token; }`.

findings.title: Chained relational operators (a < b < c) also fail to parse, same root cause as the term-chaining bug
findings.description: Consistent with the term-level chaining bug, parse_relation's post-term operator handling parses at most one additional term after a relational operator and never loops/self-recurses to check for a further relational operator, unlike parse_expression/parse_arithOp. Confirmed: 'a := 1 < 2 < 3;' fails with 'Missing ";" to end program statement'. This is a comparatively rare construct semantically (chained comparisons don't type-check well since relation-of-relation mixes bool and numeric operands under this language's rules) but is still permitted by the literal grammar and is silently mishandled rather than rejected with a clear diagnostic.
findings.evidence: parser.cpp:2146-2281 (no loop/self-recursion after the single term_parse assignment in each operator branch, e.g. 2249-2251, 2266-2267). Empirical: 'a := 1 < 2 < 3;' -> 'Error on line 4: Missing ";" to end program statement'.

findings.title: Unary minus for numbers/names is effectively implemented via arithOp's leading '-' branch, not parse_factor's dedicated (broken) branch
findings.description: Because parse_arithOp intercepts a leading '+'/'-' token before ever calling parse_relation (and thus parse_term/parse_factor), a minus sign at the very start of an arithOp chain is actually consumed by parse_arithOp's own top-level T_MINUS branch (treated as if it were a binary '<missing-left> - relation' continuation) rather than by parse_factor's dedicated '[-] number'/'[-] name' logic. This happens to make plain 'a := -5;' parse successfully purely by accident (masking the T_INTEGER_TYPE/T_FLOAT_TYPE bug documented separately), but it means: (1) the minus sign is fed to the typechecker as if it were a genuine subtraction operator missing a left operand rather than a unary-minus construct, and (2) the resulting resolved_token for the number/name never actually reflects that it was negated (no sign information is merged into the value). Since this compiler does no codegen, the practical, observable consequence today is limited to type-checking accuracy, but the architecture is fragile/inconsistent between the 'documented' unary-minus code path (parse_factor, which is broken) and the 'accidental' one that actually executes.
findings.evidence: parser.cpp:2081-2102 (parse_arithOp's own T_PLUS/T_MINUS leading branches, which call parse_relation() after consuming the sign) versus parser.cpp:2396-2429 (parse_factor's separate, broken unary-minus branch). Empirical: 'a := -5;' parses successfully at top level (arithOp intercepts the '-'), but '3 * -5' and 'x > -1' fail (parse_term/parse_relation call parse_factor() directly, exposing the T_INTEGER_TYPE/T_FLOAT_TYPE bug).

notes:
Scope covered: parser.cpp's statement dispatch (parse_base_statement), assignment/if/loop/return statement parsing, and the full expression grammar chain (parse_expression -> parse_arithOp -> parse_relation -> parse_term -> parse_factor -> parse_name / parse_procedure_call / parse_argument_list). All findings above except the last (marked speculative) were empirically reproduced by building the existing `make`-based project (pre-existing, untracked .o/binary artifacts were rebuilt via `make`; no tracked source files were modified -- `git status`/`git diff --stat` confirm a clean tree aside from the pre-existing untracked build outputs) and running the resulting `./compiler` binary against small hand-written .src test programs, with `gdb` used to get exact backtraces for the two crash findings. GCC's own `-Wreturn-type`/`-Wmaybe-uninitialized` diagnostics were used to corroborate two of the bugs (missing-return-statement crashes, uninitialized `valid_parse` in parse_relation).

The two crash findings (relational two-char operators, and 'compatible-but-unequal' return types) are the most severe: they make the compiler crash on extremely common, everyday syntax (`>=`, `<=`, `==`, `!=`, and returning an int from a bool-declared procedure), and their trigger sites are directly inside the audited functions (parse_relation, parse_return_statement), even though the ultimate defect (missing `return`) lives in Typechecker.cpp. I flagged them anyway since they are directly and trivially reachable from the statement/expression parsing code under audit.

Operator-layering itself (expression -> arithOp -> relation -> term -> factor call structure) matches the spec's precedence layers correctly; the problems found are not precedence *inversion* but (a) missing continuation loops for chained `*`/`/` and chained relational operators, (b) 'leading operator' dead-code branches at the top of parse_expression/parse_relation that accept syntactically invalid input with a missing left operand, (c) an incorrect wrong-enum comparison breaking unary minus on numeric literals in non-leading positions, (d) lost resolved_token/type information for parenthesized sub-expressions and procedure-call factors, and (e) the complete absence of undeclared-procedure/arity/argument-type checking for procedure calls, confirmed by a project that calls a fully undeclared identifier `bar(1)` and a wrong-arity/wrong-type call `foo()`/`foo(\"hello\")` with zero reported errors.

Not independently re-verified (out of assigned scope, only referenced as call sites of in-scope crashes): the internal correctness of Typechecker::token_types_compatible_at_all, check_if_statement, check_assignment_statement, and the broader SymbolTable/ScopeTable machinery. A companion 'if (isPos(5))' test additionally suggests check_return_statement mis-flags `return true;` for a bool-declared procedure as a type mismatch ('Procedure is of type \"\" ...') -- this looks like a further Typechecker-side bug but was not investigated further since it falls outside the parser statements/expressions scope.
